name: New York City
source: Catskill/Delaware and Croton reservoir systems in upstate New York; the Catskill/Delaware supply is UV-disinfected under a filtration-avoidance program
note: One of the largest unfiltered surface supplies in the U.S. Older buildings may still have lead service lines or lead solder — run the cold tap before drinking if water has sat for hours.

name: Los Angeles
utility: Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (LADWP)
source: A changing blend of the Los Angeles Aqueduct (Eastern Sierra snowmelt), imported Colorado River and State Water Project supplies, and local groundwater
note: Hardness and taste shift with the supply blend through the year. Spot scaling on fixtures is common.

name: Chicago
source: Lake Michigan, treated at the Jardine and Sawyer purification plants
note: Chicago has one of the largest counts of lead service lines in the U.S. (about 400,000 by the city's own estimate), so lead testing is especially worthwhile in older homes.

name: Houston
source: Surface water from Lake Houston, Lake Conroe and the Trinity River (Lake Livingston), plus some groundwater
note: A large surface-water system serving a fast-growing metro; boil-water notices after storms and main breaks are worth monitoring.

name: Phoenix
source: Salt and Verde rivers, Colorado River water via the Central Arizona Project, and a small share of groundwater
note: Among the hardest municipal water in the country — scale on fixtures, water heaters and kettles is the number-one complaint.

name: Philadelphia
source: Delaware and Schuylkill rivers
note: River supplies vary seasonally. Older rowhomes are a known lead-service-line risk.

name: San Antonio
source: Edwards Aquifer plus Carrizo-Wilcox groundwater and other diversified supplies
note: Very hard aquifer water. Many households use softeners; taste is generally clean.

name: San Diego
utility: City of San Diego Public Utilities Department
source: Imported Colorado River and State Water Project water, local reservoirs and desalinated seawater in the regional mix
note: Very hard imported water. Expect white scale and spotty glassware.

name: Dallas
source: Lakes Ray Hubbard, Lewisville, Grapevine, Ray Roberts, Tawakoni and Lake Fork
note: Lake-sourced supply; seasonal earthy taste can occur in late summer algae season.

name: Austin
source: Colorado River via Lake Travis and Lake Austin
note: Lime softening at the plant keeps hardness moderate for central Texas.

name: Jacksonville
source: Upper Floridan aquifer wells
note: Groundwater can carry a sulfur odor at some taps; hardness is moderate to high.

name: Columbus
utility: City of Columbus Division of Water
source: Scioto River, Big Walnut Creek and wellfields, softened at the plants
note: Spring agricultural runoff can raise nitrate in river sources; the utility monitors and blends.

name: Charlotte
source: Catawba River (Mountain Island Lake and Lake Norman)
note: Soft Piedmont surface water.

name: Indianapolis
source: White River, Fall Creek, Eagle Creek and groundwater wells
note: Very hard water typical of central Indiana's limestone geology.

name: San Francisco
source: Hetch Hetchy Reservoir (Tuolumne River) plus local Bay Area reservoirs
note: Exceptionally soft Sierra snowmelt.

name: Seattle
source: Cedar River and South Fork Tolt River watersheds
note: Very soft mountain water from protected watersheds.

name: Denver
source: Mountain snowmelt from the South Platte and Blue River systems
note: Soft to moderately hard; Denver Water runs a long-term lead reduction program.

name: Washington
utility: DC Water (treated by the Washington Aqueduct)
source: Potomac River
note: DC's 2001–2004 lead crisis drove one of the country's most watched lead service line programs.

name: Boston
source: Quabbin and Wachusett reservoirs in central Massachusetts
note: Very soft reservoir water. Older homes may have lead service lines.

name: Nashville
source: Cumberland River
note: Moderately hard river water.

name: Detroit
source: Detroit River and Lake Huron
note: Michigan's state lead rules are stricter than the federal baseline.

name: Portland
source: Bull Run watershed, with the Columbia South Shore Wellfield as backup
note: Among the softest city water in the U.S.; a new filtration facility is under construction.

name: Las Vegas
utility: Las Vegas Valley Water District (Southern Nevada Water Authority)
source: Lake Mead (Colorado River)
note: Very hard Colorado River water — softeners and RO units are common.

name: Memphis
source: Memphis Sand Aquifer (deep artesian wells)
note: Often praised for its naturally filtered aquifer water.

name: Louisville
source: Ohio River, including riverbank filtration
note: Hard river water.

name: Baltimore
utility: Baltimore City Department of Public Works
source: Loch Raven, Liberty and Prettyboy reservoirs, with the Susquehanna River as backup
note: Moderately hard reservoir water.

name: Milwaukee
source: Lake Michigan, treated with ozone
note: Milwaukee added ozone after the 1993 Cryptosporidium outbreak — one of the most studied waterborne events in U.S. history.

name: Albuquerque
utility: Albuquerque Bernalillo County Water Utility Authority
source: Rio Grande (San Juan–Chama Project water) and aquifer wells
note: Hard desert water; blend shifts between surface water and groundwater.

name: Tucson
source: Colorado River water via the Central Arizona Project (recharged and recovered) plus groundwater
note: Hard water; aquifer recharge keeps the system resilient in drought.

name: Sacramento
utility: City of Sacramento Department of Utilities
source: American and Sacramento rivers plus groundwater
note: Soft river water; groundwater areas are harder.

name: Atlanta
source: Chattahoochee River
note: Soft Piedmont river water.

name: Miami
source: Biscayne Aquifer (lime-softened) and Floridan Aquifer
note: Softened at the plant; saltwater intrusion into the aquifer is a long-term concern.

name: Tampa
source: Hillsborough River, with aquifer and regional supplies
note: Hard water; taste can change in dry season.

name: Orlando
source: Lower Floridan aquifer, treated with ozone
note: Ozone treatment removes the sulfur taste common in Florida groundwater.

name: Minneapolis
utility: City of Minneapolis Water Treatment and Distribution
source: Mississippi River, lime-softened
note: Softened river water; seasonal taste changes in spring.

name: Kansas City
source: Missouri River
note: Hard river water; the region surrounding the city has some of the hardest supplies in the Midwest.

name: St. Louis
utility: City of St. Louis Water Division
source: Missouri and Mississippi rivers
note: River water treated at the Chain of Rocks and Howard Bend plants.

name: New Orleans
utility: Sewerage and Water Board of New Orleans
source: Mississippi River
note: Boil-water advisories follow pressure drops — keep an eye on alerts.

name: Salt Lake City
utility: Salt Lake City Department of Public Utilities
source: Wasatch canyon streams (City Creek, Parley's, Big Cottonwood) plus wells
note: Hard mountain-and-well water; blends vary by neighbourhood.

name: Pittsburgh
source: Allegheny River
note: Pittsburgh runs an active lead service line replacement program.

name: Cleveland
source: Lake Erie
note: Late-summer algal blooms in Lake Erie are monitored closely.

name: Oklahoma City
source: Lakes Hefner, Overholser and Draper, fed by Atoka and McGee Creek reservoirs
note: Hard lake water; taste and odor events can occur in summer.

name: Raleigh
source: Falls Lake and Lake Benson
note: Soft Piedmont lake water.

name: Honolulu
source: Basal groundwater aquifers on Oʻahu
note: Naturally filtered groundwater; aquifer protection is a top local issue.

name: Anchorage
source: Eklutna Lake and Ship Creek
note: Very soft glacial-fed water.

name: Fort Worth
source: Eagle Mountain, Benbrook, Richland-Chambers and Cedar Creek lakes
note: Lake water; seasonal earthy taste can occur.

name: Boise
source: Boise River plus groundwater wells
note: Hardness varies by well zone.

name: Toronto
source: Lake Ontario
note: Moderately hard lake water. Health Canada's lead guideline (5 µg/L) is stricter than the U.S. action level; Toronto offers free lead test kits.

name: Montréal
utility: Service de l'eau, Ville de Montréal
source: St. Lawrence River and Rivière des Prairies
note: Montréal is replacing its lead service lines city-wide; residents in pre-1970 homes should check their entrance pipe.

name: Vancouver
source: Capilano, Seymour and Coquitlam reservoirs
note: Very soft rainforest water — naturally corrosive, so the region adds corrosion control.

name: Calgary
source: Bow and Elbow rivers
note: Hard water; scale is common in kettles and water heaters.

name: Ottawa
source: Ottawa River
note: Soft river water.

name: Edmonton
source: North Saskatchewan River
note: Hard prairie river water; spring runoff changes taste.

name: Winnipeg
source: Shoal Lake via a gravity aqueduct
note: Treated at the Deacon plant; moderately hard.

name: Québec City
source: Saint-Charles River and the St. Lawrence River
note: Soft surface water.

name: Halifax
source: Pockwock Lake and Lake Major
note: Very soft lake water.

name: London
source: River Thames, River Lee and chalk aquifers
note: Some of the hardest water in Britain — limescale is a way of life.

name: Manchester
source: Lake District reservoirs (Haweswater and Thirlmere)
note: Very soft upland water.

name: Paris
source: Groundwater springs plus the Seine and Marne rivers
note: Hard water from chalk and limestone sources.

name: Sydney
source: Warragamba Dam and other protected catchments
note: Soft surface water.

name: Melbourne
source: Protected forested catchments such as the Thomson and Upper Yarra reservoirs
note: Very soft water from closed catchments.
